lead: A pulsed radar cannot listen while it transmits, so it sends a pulse and waits a fixed time for the echo. The pulse repetition frequency (PRF) sets that waiting time, and therefore the longest range the radar can measure without confusing one pulse's echo with another. This is why PRF is chosen before waveform timing, and why it controls both range ambiguity and the radar's power budget. Air-traffic radars, weather radars and military search radars all pick PRF around this compromise.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for maximum range Rmax, and Chapter 6.1 for echo timing.

blocks.text: A pulsed radar sends a short pulse, then switches to receive. It waits one pulse repetition time T<sub>r</sub> before the next pulse. PRF is the number of pulses per second. The period is T<sub>r</sub> = 1 / PRF. The transmitter is on for τ of that period, so the receiver listens for T<sub>r</sub> − τ. An echo must return inside this listening time. If it returns later, the next pulse has already gone out and the receiver cannot tell which pulse produced it.
T<sub>r</sub> = 1 / PRF,   R<sub>unamb</sub> = c T<sub>r</sub> / 2 = c / (2 PRF)
blocks.where: T<sub>r</sub> is the pulse repetition time in seconds; PRF is in hertz; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light; R<sub>unamb</sub> is the unambiguous range in metres. The factor 2 is the out-and-back path. In a simple pulsed radar τ is much smaller than T<sub>r</sub>, so the listening time T<sub>r</sub> − τ is taken as T<sub>r</sub> itself.

blocks.text: The pulse width τ is the on-time of each pulse. Duty cycle is the fraction of time the transmitter is on: τ / T<sub>r</sub> = τ PRF. Average power is P<sub>av</sub> = P<sub>t</sub> τ PRF, where P<sub>t</sub> is peak power. A radar with P<sub>t</sub> = 1 MW, τ = 1 μs and PRF = 1 kHz has duty cycle 0.001 and P<sub>av</sub> = 1 kW.

The table and figure show the same law: doubling PRF halves R<sub>unamb</sub>. At 100 Hz the radar can listen for 10 ms, so R<sub>unamb</sub> = 1500 km. At 10 kHz it listens for 100 μs, so R<sub>unamb</sub> = 15 km.

A target beyond R<sub>unamb</sub> still gives an echo. The echo arrives after the next pulse is sent. The radar measures only the delay inside one period, so the target folds back. For one extra period, apparent range R<sub>app</sub> = R − R<sub>unamb</sub>. For n extra periods, R<sub>app</sub> = R − n R<sub>unamb</sub>, with n a whole number. A target at 200 km with R<sub>unamb</sub> = 150 km appears at 50 km.

Eclipsing happens when the echo arrives while the radar is transmitting. The receiver is blanked or sees only the strong leakage pulse, so the target is missed. The smallest measurable range is set by pulse width and receiver recovery: R<sub>blind</sub> = c τ / 2 plus recovery distance. A 1 μs pulse gives R<sub>blind</sub> = 150 m before recovery is added.

blocks.where: τ is the pulse width in seconds; t<sub>rec</sub> is the receiver recovery time in seconds; R<sub>blind</sub> is the blind range in metres.

blocks.text: Range gating divides the listening window into bins. Each gate is a short sampling window of width τ (the pulse width) in time, which corresponds to a range-bin width of c τ / 2 metres. Bin k covers range near k c τ / 2. The display or processor uses these bins for thresholding, tracking and clutter maps. A long pulse gives coarse bins and a large blind range; a short pulse gives fine bins but less energy per pulse.

High PRF means short T<sub>r</sub>, so R<sub>unamb</sub> is small and range is ambiguous. But pulses come often, so Doppler shift is sampled often and target velocity can be unambiguous over a wide span. Low PRF gives long T<sub>r</sub>, large R<sub>unamb</sub>, but Doppler is ambiguous. Medium PRF sits between. Search radars often use low or medium PRF; pulse Doppler fire-control radars use high or medium PRF.

items: High PRF: good Doppler, poor range.
Low PRF: good range, poor Doppler.
Medium PRF: both are partly ambiguous.

blocks.text: Multiple PRF sets resolve both. The radar transmits groups of pulses at two or more PRFs. A true target appears at a consistent true range after unfolding; a false fold does not. Staggered PRF changes the period from pulse to pulse so second-time-around echoes land at different apparent ranges and can be rejected. See Chapter 6.6 for blind speeds and staggered PRF, and Chapter 6.5 for Doppler ambiguity.

figure.caption: Unambiguous range falls as 1/PRF: 1500 km at 100 Hz, 150 km at 1 kHz, 15 km at 10 kHz. The worked example sits at 1 kHz.

spec.aria: Curve showing that the unambiguous range falls as one over the pulse repetition frequency, from 1500 km at 100 Hz down to 15 km at 10 kHz.

examples.question: A radar works at PRF = 1000 Hz with a pulse width of 1 μs. Find T<sub>r</sub>, the duty cycle, the unambiguous range and the blind range. A target is actually at 200 km. Where does the radar place it?
steps: Duty cycle = τ / T<sub>r</sub> = (1 × 10⁻⁶ s) / (1 × 10⁻³ s) = 1 × 10⁻³ = 0.001 = 0.1 per cent.
R<sub>unamb</sub> = c T<sub>r</sub> / 2 = (3 × 10⁸ m/s × 1 × 10⁻³ s) / 2 = 150000 m = 150 km.
R<sub>blind</sub> = c τ / 2 = (3 × 10⁸ m/s × 1 × 10⁻⁶ s) / 2 = 150 m.
Target at 200 km exceeds R<sub>unamb</sub> = 150 km. Apparent range = 200 km − 150 km = 50 km.
examples.answer: T<sub>r</sub> = 1 ms, duty cycle = 0.001 (0.1 per cent), R<sub>unamb</sub> = 150 km, R<sub>blind</sub> = 150 m, and the 200 km target appears at 50 km.
examples.check:
prf = 1000.0
tau = 1e-6
c = 3e8
Tr = 1.0/prf
duty = tau/Tr
Runamb = c*Tr/2.0
blind = c*tau/2.0
R = 200e3
apparent = R - Runamb
print(Tr)
print(duty)
print(Runamb/1000.0)
print(blind)
print(apparent/1000.0)

traps: Dropping the factor 2 and writing R<sub>unamb</sub> = c / PRF. The wave must travel out and back inside one repetition period.
Using pulse width τ in place of repetition time T<sub>r</sub>. τ sets blind range and range-bin width; T<sub>r</sub> sets unambiguous range.
Treating a second-time-around echo as noise. It is a real echo folded by R − n R<sub>unamb</sub>.
Thinking high PRF is always better. High PRF improves Doppler but makes range ambiguous.
Confusing PRF with pulse width or bandwidth. PRF controls range ambiguity; pulse width controls blind range and range resolution.

quiz.q: Define PRF and give its relation to T<sub>r</sub>.
quiz.a: PRF is the number of pulses transmitted per second. T<sub>r</sub> = 1 / PRF.

quiz.q: Why does the unambiguous range formula contain a factor 2?
quiz.a: The wave travels from radar to target and back, so the path length is 2R. The round-trip delay is 2R/c.

quiz.q: A radar has PRF = 2000 Hz. Find R<sub>unamb</sub>. Take c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
quiz.a: T<sub>r</sub> = 1/2000 = 0.5 ms. R<sub>unamb</sub> = c T<sub>r</sub>/2 = 3 × 10⁸ × 0.5 × 10⁻³ / 2 = 75 km.

quiz.q: A radar has peak power 500 kW, pulse width 2 μs and PRF 500 Hz. Find duty cycle and average power.
quiz.a: Duty cycle = τ PRF = 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 500 = 0.001. P<sub>av</sub> = P<sub>t</sub> × duty = 500 kW × 0.001 = 500 W.

quiz.q: A target is at 120 km. The radar PRF is 2000 Hz. What range is displayed, and why?
quiz.a: R<sub>unamb</sub> = 75 km. The target exceeds one period, so R<sub>app</sub> = 120 − 75 = 45 km.

quiz.q: Compare high PRF and low PRF for range ambiguity and Doppler ambiguity.
quiz.a: High PRF gives small unambiguous range but wide unambiguous Doppler. Low PRF gives large unambiguous range but ambiguous Doppler.

quiz.q: Why do radars use multiple PRFs or staggered PRF?
quiz.a: Different PRFs fold a true target to different apparent ranges. Comparing groups resolves the true range, and staggered PRF helps reject second-time-around echoes and blind-speed nulls.

quiz.q: Write the blind range formula in terms of pulse width.
quiz.a: R<sub>blind</sub> = c τ / 2, plus a term for receiver recovery time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern radars use pulse compression to separate pulse width from range resolution, so a long pulse can still give fine range bins. Medium-PRF and multiple-PRF schedules are common in airborne pulse Doppler sets. Digital processors unfold range and Doppler jointly and reject second-time-around echoes automatically. Search next for medium PRF radar, staggered PRF, and range-Doppler ambiguity resolution.
